foodDescription: A small cake baked in a fluted copper mold, with a dark caramelized crust and a soft center flavored with rum and vanilla. Said to have been made by nuns with egg yolks left over from clarifying wine.
Grilled rib steak with a sauce of red wine, shallots, and bone marrow, sometimes grilled over vine cuttings.
Lamprey, an eel-like fish from the Gironde estuary, stewed in red wine with leeks and its own blood. A spring specialty, and an acquired taste.
Oysters from the Bay of Arcachon, an hour west of the city, eaten raw, often with small grilled sausages on the side.
Wild porcini sautéed in oil with garlic, shallots, and parsley. Picked in the forests around Bordeaux in autumn.
Milk-fed lamb from the Médoc, traditionally raised among the vineyards of Pauillac, roasted pink.
A cold roll of seasoned pork stomach, sliced thin like charcuterie. A specialty of the Médoc.
Simple, chewy almond cookies baked on paper, made in Saint-Émilion since the 1600s, older than the colorful Paris kind.
A light choux bun filled with whipped cream, created in the 2000s at Cap Ferret on the coast and now sold in Bordeaux.
What the rest of France calls a pain au chocolat. In Bordeaux and the southwest, calling it anything else starts an argument.
A golden dessert wine from grapes shriveled by a beneficial mold, grown south of the city. Often served with foie gras.
An aperitif of Bordeaux wine and fruit liqueurs, made in Podensac, just south of the city, since 1872. Served chilled with orange.
